source: Durian Orchard (ការដាំធូរេន), by Vann Thana Busab and Montry Vong Phanith, published by the Northwest Cambodia Provinces Fruit Culture Development Committee (Battambang), 1998, 59pp, AIDOC code 178-001
text:
Correctly judging fruit maturity is one of the most important and trickiest skills in durian growing, since fruit cut too early will never ripen properly and fruit left too long may split, over-ripen on the tree, or fall and be damaged. This source gives approximate days-from-flowering-to-maturity counts for the four variety types it describes, though it cautions that a grower should still confirm ripeness with a physical maturity check (see below) rather than relying on the day-count alone, since it can vary somewhat with weather and tree vigor:

Kra Dao Khmum type: about 90-100 days from flowering to maturity.
Aak Ni type: about 110-120 days.
Kan Yeav (long-stalk) type: about 120-135 days.
Mon Chong type: about 140-150 days.

The source explicitly flags that this day-count method carries some risk of error (its own text uses the English word 'ERROR' at this point) because weather that is unusually hot and dry, or a run of heavy storms, can shift the timeline earlier or later than the average. It recommends that growers keep a written, dated record of when each cluster flowered so the count can be tracked accurately per cluster, and cross-check the day count against physical maturity signs before cutting.
